title: A Peace Deal Could Be Signed This Weekend. India's Markets Just Had Their Best Day in Two Months.
excerpt: Brent crude fell to its lowest since March, the Sensex surged 2.3 per cent, and the rupee rallied to 95.11 — all on a deal that has not actually been signed yet.
body:
The war that has rewritten India's economic story for three months may be about to end — on paper, at least.

A memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran could be signed as early as Sunday, a Western source told Reuters on Friday, with Geneva emerging as the likeliest venue. The agreement would be signed by US Vice President JD Vance and Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf, with Pakistan serving as mediator.

"The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding has never been closer," Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on X on Friday. Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif followed minutes later: "A final, agreed upon text of the peace deal has been reached."

Indian markets responded before any ink had dried.

## The Best Day in Months

The BSE Sensex surged 2.3 per cent to 75,527.95, its strongest single-day gain since April. The Nifty 50 jumped 1.99 per cent to 23,622.90. Brent crude fell to $85.80 a barrel — its lowest in three months — before settling at $87.33, down 3.37 per cent on the day. WTI crude dropped to $84.88, its lowest since April 17.

The rally broke a two-week losing streak for India's benchmarks and buoyed sectors hammered by the conflict. Oil marketing companies, airlines, tyre makers, paint manufacturers, and cement companies all gained sharply. Financials led, boosted by the RBI's recent decision to ease overseas borrowing rules. Kotak Mahindra Bank, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank were among the top weekly gainers, rising about 6.9, 6.2, and 3.4 per cent respectively.

The rupee, Asia's second-worst performing currency this year with a 6 per cent decline, clawed back Thursday's losses. It climbed to a one-week high of 94.9550 before settling at 95.11, up 0.7 per cent on the day.

"The decline in crude prices, easing geopolitical fears have helped sentiment recover and this could continue in the near term," said Rajesh Palviya, head of research at Axis Direct.

## What the Deal Contains

Draft terms described to Reuters by multiple sources indicate that the US would immediately begin releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on its oil exports, in return for Iran opening the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's nuclear programme would be addressed during a 60-day period of talks. A senior US official said the agreement would ultimately lead to the dismantling of Iran's nuclear programme, with its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to be "destroyed and removed." The terms also include discussion of possible war reparations for Tehran and the dropping of longstanding US demands for limits on Iran's missile programme.

But the terms appear to give Tehran much of what it demanded. Nuclear issues are deferred. Iran's missile programme is excluded from the immediate deal. Sanctions would be waived and frozen assets released. The cessation of hostilities would extend to Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting Iran-backed Hezbollah.

Trump blasted the terms leaked by Iranian media, posting on Truth Social that they had "NOTHING to do with the terms that were agreed to." He called Iran "very dishonourable people to deal with."

## What It Means for India

India, the world's third-largest oil importer, has been one of the countries most exposed to the war. The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of global oil and LNG shipments before the conflict. Its effective closure sent Brent crude above $100 a barrel, pushed India's May inflation to a new-series high of 3.93 per cent, and forced state-owned fuel retailers to raise prices four times in a single month.

The government is already bracing for the fiscal fallout. Bloomberg reported this week that India is preparing to let its budget deficit widen to 4.8 per cent of GDP, up from the 4.3 per cent target set in February, as energy subsidy costs balloon.

Foreign investors have pulled a record $30 billion from Indian equities this year, pushing the country's market capitalisation below both South Korea and Taiwan for the first time. BlackRock said this week that India had been "over-punished."

If the deal holds and the strait reopens, analysts say the reversal could be swift. Kotak Mahindra Bank expects the rupee to move towards 93.0-93.5 in the months ahead. Lighthouse Canton believes foreign outflows may have largely run their course.

But there is a caveat. Global and regional oil stocks remain low, and even with a signed deal it would take time to ensure uninterrupted oil flows. "Headlines are driving the market once again as confidence grows that an eventual deal will be struck," said Tamas Varga, an analyst at PVM Oil Associates. The deal, if it arrives, would mark the most significant diplomatic breakthrough since the war began in late February. For India, it would end the most damaging external shock since the pandemic.
image_caption: A stock market screen showing numbers and data — Indian benchmarks logged their best session in two months on Friday
nri_angle: For NRIs with Indian market investments, rupee-denominated assets, or family back home dealing with rising fuel and food costs, a peace deal could reverse months of damage — but the terms still favour Tehran.
author: Diaspora Desk
